Benito Juárez. The Zapotec Mexican president who led the country through the Reform War and French intervention, ultimately restoring the republic in 1867. He championed liberal democratic principles and indigenous rights, transforming Mexico from monarchy back to a federal republic.

Juárez rose from a poor Zapotec background in Oaxaca to become Mexico's first indigenous president. He led the Reform War from 1858 to 1861 against conservative forces, establishing liberal governance and secular authority over the church. During the French intervention from 1861 to 1867, he resisted the foreign-imposed emperor Maximilian I and reclaimed Mexico City. To build a secular state, he issued the Laws of Reform, which stripped the church of land and political power. He became known for his motto: "Respect for the rights of others is peace," a founding principle of Mexican liberalism. After his victories, Juárez won reelection in 1867 and again in 1871, implementing educational reform and modernisation before his death in 1872. His vision of secular governance stood in contrast to the monarchical experiment of Maximilian, and he carried forward the indigenous advocacy that Benito's predecessor, Miguel Hidalgo, had embodied in the independence struggle.
